note: Reference data for Iconographer, a Christian iconography app. Each entry is a single symbol -- a gesture, pose, object, animal, plant, garment, color, monogram, or scene type -- with a meaning that stands on its own. 'figures' is optional context (which Christian figures/scenes this symbol is commonly associated with), never required to explain the symbol. 'aliases' catches plain-English phrasings a vision model is likely to use. Expand freely; keep 'name' and 'aliases' lowercase and specific.

symbols.name: benediction gesture (Latin)
symbols.meaning: A raised right hand with the thumb, index, and middle finger extended and the last two folded into the palm is the Western gesture of blessing. The three raised fingers are read as the Trinity and the two folded ones as the dual nature of Christ, so the hand is a small creed as well as a blessing. It signals sacred authority and divine favor conferred on the viewer.

figures.name: Christ Pantocrator
figures.note: the standard hand of the enthroned, all-ruling Christ

figures.name: Bishops and popes
figures.note: shows the sitter exercising priestly authority

symbols.name: benediction gesture (Greek/Byzantine)
symbols.meaning: In Eastern Orthodox icons the blessing hand is shaped so the fingers spell the Greek letters ΙϹ ΧϹ — an abbreviation of 'Jesus Christ.' The gesture is simultaneously a blessing and a monogram naming the one who gives it.

figures.name: Christ (Orthodox icons)
figures.note: near-universal hand position in Byzantine and Russian icons

symbols.name: orans / orant pose
symbols.meaning: Both arms raised to shoulder height with palms open and facing outward is one of the oldest prayer postures in Western art, inherited from pagan antiquity. In early Christian catacomb painting it marks a soul at prayer, often standing for the deceased interceding in paradise.

figures.name: Early Christian catacomb figures
figures.note: the standard pose for the departed soul in 3rd–4th century funerary art

figures.name: The Virgin Orans
figures.note: an icon type showing Mary in this pose, sometimes with Christ in a roundel on her breast

symbols.name: Ecce Homo presentation
symbols.meaning: A bound, scourged figure in a crown of thorns and mock robe being gestured toward by another shows the moment Pilate presents Christ to the crowd with the words 'Ecce homo' ('Behold the man'). The open presenting hand is what identifies the scene.

figures.name: Christ
figures.note: the one presented, crowned with thorns in a mock purple robe

figures.name: Pontius Pilate
figures.note: makes the presenting gesture, often while washing his hands nearby

symbols.name: hand on chest / heart
symbols.meaning: A hand laid flat on the chest signals sincerity, piety, or inward devotion — attention turned toward the figure's own soul rather than outward at the viewer. It is common in portraits of saints and pious donors to convey heartfelt faith or an oath of loyalty.

figures.name: Counter-Reformation saints
figures.note: a recurring gesture of interior devotion, especially in El Greco

symbols.name: striking the breast
symbols.meaning: A closed fist struck against the chest is the gesture of penitence and self-accusation — the 'mea culpa' of the repentant sinner or the publican in the parable who would not raise his eyes. Distinct from the open, flat hand of sincerity.

figures.name: Penitent figures
figures.note: Mary Magdalene, Saint Peter after his denial, and the publican

symbols.name: index finger raised upward
symbols.meaning: A single finger aimed at heaven directs attention to divine truth, prophecy, or the world beyond — 'look up, look past this.' It marks a figure as prophet, teacher, or philosopher concerned with eternal rather than earthly things.

figures.name: Saint John the Baptist
figures.note: points upward or toward Christ to announce the coming Messiah

figures.name: Plato (School of Athens)
figures.note: points to the heavens for his philosophy of eternal ideal forms

symbols.name: hands clasped in prayer
symbols.meaning: Palms pressed together with fingers aligned or interlaced is the standard Western gesture of devout prayer, distinct from the older open-armed orans pose. Its origin lies in the feudal gesture of a vassal placing joined hands between a lord's — prayer as an act of homage.

figures.name: Donor portraits
figures.note: patrons who paid for an altarpiece kneel at its edge with hands clasped

symbols.name: averted or downcast gaze
symbols.meaning: Eyes lowered or turned from the viewer signal humility, modesty, or penitence, distinguishing quiet inward reflection from the direct outward gaze used for authority or witness.

figures.name: The Penitent Magdalene
figures.note: downcast eyes reinforce sorrow and repentance

figures.name: The Virgin at the Annunciation
figures.note: modesty and submission at the angel's greeting

symbols.name: drawing back from a touch
symbols.meaning: A risen figure pulling away from a kneeling woman's outstretched hand depicts 'Noli me tangere' ('Do not hold on to me'), Christ's words to Mary Magdalene in the garden after the Resurrection. The withheld touch marks a body no longer belonging to ordinary earthly contact.

figures.name: Christ and Mary Magdalene
figures.note: Christ often carries a gardener's hoe, since she first mistook him for the gardener

symbols.name: finger probing a wound
symbols.meaning: A man placing his finger into the side wound of a risen figure is the Doubting Thomas — the apostle who refused to believe without physical proof. The gesture is about the demand for tangible evidence and its rebuke: 'blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.'

figures.name: Saint Thomas the Apostle
figures.note: his defining moment and the origin of 'doubting Thomas'

symbols.name: head resting on the hand
symbols.meaning: A seated figure propping the head on one hand is the ancient sign of melancholy, grief, or deep thought. In Renaissance art it becomes the signature pose of the melancholic temperament, associated with genius, artistic inspiration, and creative paralysis alike.

figures.name: Mourners
figures.note: the same pose marks grief at a deposition or entombment

symbols.name: covering the face with hands
symbols.meaning: Hands raised to hide the face express grief too great to show, or shame. Classical writers praised a painter who veiled a father's face at his daughter's sacrifice because no depiction could equal the sorrow implied, and the device recurs whenever an artist wants emotion beyond depiction.

figures.name: Mourning figures
figures.note: at a Lamentation, Massacre of the Innocents, or Expulsion from Eden

symbols.name: hands shielding the body (pudica)
symbols.meaning: A nude figure covering breast and groin with her hands is the 'pudica' (modest) pose inherited from classical Venus statues. The gesture simultaneously conceals and draws attention, and painters use it to frame nudity as chaste rather than lascivious.

figures.name: Eve
figures.note: adopted for Eve's shame after the Fall

symbols.name: bound hands
symbols.meaning: Wrists tied with rope or cord mark a captive, prisoner, or figure delivered up for judgment and execution. In martyrdom imagery the binding emphasizes helplessness willingly accepted rather than resisted.

figures.name: Christ before Pilate
figures.note: bound during the Passion

figures.name: Saint Sebastian
figures.note: bound to a tree or column for his martyrdom

symbols.name: arms crossed over the chest
symbols.meaning: Arms folded across the breast signal humble submission and acceptance of God's will. It is the standard attitude of the Virgin accepting the Annunciation and of the Immaculate Conception, and in Orthodox practice the posture for receiving communion.

figures.name: The Virgin Mary
figures.note: 'be it unto me according to thy word' — assent at the Annunciation

symbols.name: contrapposto stance
symbols.meaning: A standing figure with weight shifted onto one leg, hips and shoulders counter-rotated into a relaxed S-curve. Invented in classical Greece and revived in the Renaissance, it signals naturalism, ease, and idealized grace as opposed to rigid frontal formality.

figures.name: Classical and Renaissance sculpture
figures.note: the defining stance of the idealized standing nude from Polykleitos to Michelangelo

symbols.name: veiled or covered head
symbols.meaning: A head covered by veil, hood, or drawn mantle signals mourning, modesty, or ritual solemnity. Widows, penitents, and figures present at a death or sacrifice are commonly veiled; in Roman practice covering the head marked the moment of performing a rite.

figures.name: Mourning figures
figures.note: veiling at a Deposition or Entombment marks grief

symbols.name: kneeling pose
symbols.meaning: A figure on one or both knees signals submission, homage, prayer, or adoration — lowering the body beneath another's level to mark reverence, whether religious devotion or earthly fealty.

figures.name: The Magi and shepherds
figures.note: kneeling marks worship of the infant Christ

figures.name: Donors
figures.note: patrons kneel at the margins of the sacred scene they commissioned

symbols.name: enthroned figure
symbols.meaning: A frontal figure seated on a throne, usually raised on steps and larger than surrounding figures, asserts sovereignty and majesty. In a sacred setting the throne turns a portrait into a statement of rule over heaven and earth.

figures.name: The Virgin and Child in Majesty
figures.note: the 'Maestà' type, with Mary enthroned as Queen of Heaven and seat of Wisdom

figures.name: Christ in Majesty
figures.note: enthroned as judge and ruler of all

symbols.name: trampling a figure underfoot
symbols.meaning: A victorious figure standing on a prostrate enemy, serpent, or demon is the visual formula for total conquest — evil not merely defeated but placed beneath the feet. Crushing a serpent's head specifically echoes the promise in Genesis that the woman's offspring would bruise the serpent.

figures.name: Saint Michael
figures.note: stands on Satan as dragon or demon

figures.name: The Immaculate Virgin
figures.note: treads on the serpent, and often a crescent moon

symbols.name: swooning or fainting figure
symbols.meaning: A figure sinking backward, supported by companions, conveys grief so overwhelming it overcomes the body. In Passion scenes this is the 'Spasimo' — the Virgin fainting at the sight of her son — a motif that let painters give her a share in his suffering.

figures.name: The Virgin Mary
figures.note: swooning on the road to Calvary or beneath the cross

symbols.name: figure carrying its own severed head
symbols.meaning: A standing, headless figure holding its own head is a 'cephalophore.' The impossible image asserts that martyrdom did not end the saint's mission — several were said to have walked and preached after decapitation.

figures.name: Saint Denis
figures.note: carried his head from Montmartre after beheading; patron of Paris

symbols.name: figures sheltered under an outspread cloak
symbols.meaning: A large central figure holding open a cloak to shelter small kneeling people beneath it is the 'Madonna of Mercy' formula. Scale here is hierarchical rather than spatial — the protector is painted large because she matters most, not because she is nearer.

figures.name: The Virgin of Mercy
figures.note: shelters a confraternity, city, or religious order under her mantle

figures.name: Saint Ursula
figures.note: shelters her virgin companions the same way

symbols.name: child carried on the shoulder across water
aliases: giant carrying a child through a river
man fording water with child on shoulders
symbols.meaning: A large figure wading through water with a small child on one shoulder, leaning on a staff, depicts the ferryman who unknowingly carried the Christ Child and found him impossibly heavy — the weight of the world's sin.

figures.name: Saint Christopher
figures.note: his name means 'Christ-bearer'; patron of travelers

symbols.name: halo / nimbus
aliases: ring of light around the head
symbols.meaning: A ring or disc of light around the head marks sanctity — the figure is recognized as holy, blessed, or divine. Its shape carries further information: plain and round for saints, and other forms reserved for specific persons.

figures.name: Saints generally
figures.note: the universal shorthand for holiness across nearly all Christian art

symbols.name: halo with a cross inside it
symbols.meaning: A halo containing the arms of a cross is reserved for Christ alone (and by extension for the Lamb or the Trinity's persons). Seeing one settles the identity of a figure that might otherwise be read as any saint.

figures.name: Christ
figures.note: the single most reliable identifier of Christ in Christian art

symbols.name: square or rectangular halo
symbols.meaning: A square halo marks a person who was still alive when the image was made — used chiefly for popes and donors in early medieval Rome. It carefully distinguishes the merely eminent from the canonized dead, who get round haloes.

figures.name: Living donors and popes
figures.note: an explicit signal that the sitter had not yet died, let alone been canonized

symbols.name: triangular halo
symbols.meaning: A three-sided halo signifies the Trinity and is reserved for God the Father. The geometry does the theological work: one figure, three equal sides.

figures.name: God the Father
figures.note: distinguishes him from Christ, who receives the cross-marked halo

symbols.name: almond-shaped body halo (mandorla)
aliases: almond of light around a figure
symbols.meaning: An almond-shaped field of light enclosing an entire figure, not just the head. It signals a body in glory or in transit between heaven and earth, and so appears at moments of revelation or bodily ascent.

figures.name: Christ
figures.note: at the Transfiguration, Ascension, and in Majesty

figures.name: The Virgin
figures.note: at her Assumption

symbols.name: wings
symbols.meaning: Wings mark a figure as more than human — an angel, a personification, or a divine messenger able to move between the earthly and heavenly realms. On an allegorical figure they usually indicate swiftness or the transcendence of ordinary limits.

figures.name: Angels and archangels
figures.note: the defining mark distinguishing them from human saints

symbols.name: winged man (evangelist symbol)
symbols.meaning: One of the four evangelist symbols. A winged human figure identifies the Gospel that opens by tracing Christ's human ancestry, and can be shown dictating to the writer.

figures.name: Saint Matthew the Evangelist
figures.note: his Gospel begins with the human genealogy of Christ

symbols.name: stigmata
symbols.meaning: Wounds appearing on the hands, feet, and side, matching the injuries of the crucifixion, mark a figure as having received a mystical identification with Christ's suffering rather than an ordinary injury.

figures.name: Saint Francis of Assisi
figures.note: received them in a vision of a winged seraph; the first documented case

figures.name: Saint Catherine of Siena
figures.note: traditionally shown with invisible or rayed stigmata

symbols.name: flaming heart
symbols.meaning: A heart wrapped in flame stands for ardent divine love — charity burning rather than merely felt. Held in the hand it is an attribute; worn on the breast it can indicate the Sacred Heart devotion.

figures.name: Saint Augustine
figures.note: his usual attribute, sometimes pierced by an arrow

figures.name: Charity personified
figures.note: the flame marks love as the theological virtue

symbols.name: heart pierced by swords
symbols.meaning: A heart transfixed by one or (more often) seven blades signifies the sorrows of the Virgin, from Simeon's prophecy that 'a sword shall pierce through thy own soul.' Seven is the count of her traditional Sorrows, from the flight into Egypt to the entombment.

figures.name: The Mater Dolorosa
figures.note: Our Lady of Sorrows, shown weeping with swords at her breast

symbols.name: tonsure (shaved crown of the head)
aliases: shaved head with ring of hair
bald crown with hair around it
symbols.meaning: A shaved patch on the crown, leaving a ring of hair, marks a man as a monk or cleric. The exposed circle was read as a crown of thorns and a renunciation of vanity.

figures.name: Monastic saints
figures.note: combined with the habit's color, it helps identify the specific order

symbols.name: blindfold
symbols.meaning: A blindfolded personification with covered eyes staring blankly ahead is Synagoga — the Synagogue depicted as failing to see and accept Christ, often paired opposite a crowned, clear-eyed Ecclesia (the Church). A common, pointed figure in medieval church sculpture and stained glass.

figures.name: Synagoga
figures.note: a personification of the Synagogue blindfolded to signify failure to recognize Christ — a hostile medieval trope

symbols.name: Chi-Rho monogram
aliases: P with an X through it
symbols.meaning: The superimposed Greek letters Chi (Χ) and Rho (Ρ), the first two of ΧΡΙΣΤΟΣ, form the oldest Christogram. Adopted by Constantine as a military standard, it functions as both an abbreviation of Christ's name and a sign of victory.

figures.name: Christ
figures.note: often flanked by alpha and omega on sarcophagi and apse mosaics

symbols.name: IHS monogram
symbols.meaning: The letters IHS abbreviate ΙΗΣΟΥΣ, the Greek spelling of Jesus, using its first three letters. Later readings expanded it into Latin phrases such as 'Iesus Hominum Salvator,' but the origin is simply the name.

figures.name: Saint Bernardino of Siena
figures.note: holds a tablet with IHS in a blazing sun, the emblem he preached with

figures.name: The Jesuits
figures.note: adopted it as the emblem of the Society of Jesus

symbols.name: INRI inscription
symbols.meaning: The board fixed above the cross reading INRI — 'Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudaeorum,' Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews. Written as a legal charge, it is preserved in Christian art as an unintended proclamation of kingship.

figures.name: The Crucifixion
figures.note: the placard Pilate ordered fixed to the cross

symbols.name: alpha and omega
aliases: first and last letters of the greek alphabet
symbols.meaning: The first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, flanking a figure or Christogram, declare 'I am the beginning and the end' — divinity encompassing all of time.

figures.name: Christ
figures.note: usually paired with the Chi-Rho or shown beside Christ in Majesty

symbols.name: crown of thorns
aliases: circle of thorns on the head
symbols.meaning: A twisted ring of thorn branches, forced onto the head as a parody of a royal wreath during the mockery before the crucifixion. It fuses kingship and humiliation into one object and is a central instrument of the Passion.

figures.name: Christ
figures.note: worn from the mockery through the crucifixion

figures.name: Penitent saints
figures.note: occasionally held or worn in imitation of Christ's suffering

symbols.name: three nails
symbols.meaning: Three long iron nails belong to the Arma Christi, the instruments of the Passion, displayed as objects of devotion. The count of three reflects the common medieval convention of feet crossed and pinned by a single nail.

figures.name: The Passion of Christ
figures.note: held by angels or arranged around the cross in devotional images

symbols.name: hammer and pincers
aliases: hammer and tongs by a cross
symbols.meaning: A hammer to drive the nails in and pincers to draw them out, paired among the instruments of the Passion. Together they compress the crucifixion and the deposition into two tools.

figures.name: The Passion of Christ
figures.note: part of the Arma Christi, often held by attending angels

symbols.name: lance or spear (piercing the side)
symbols.meaning: The spear that pierced the side of the crucified Christ, releasing blood and water. As a Passion instrument it stands for the wound that confirmed death and, in Eucharistic reading, the source of the sacraments.

figures.name: Saint Longinus
figures.note: the centurion who made the thrust and was converted by it

symbols.name: sponge on a reed
symbols.meaning: A sponge soaked in vinegar and raised on a long reed to the mouth of the crucified — offered as drink and received as one more indignity. It belongs to the instruments of the Passion, usually shown crossed with the lance.

figures.name: The Crucifixion
figures.note: typically paired with the lance to flank the cross

symbols.name: column with scourge or whip
symbols.meaning: A short column with a whip or bundle of rods is the site and instrument of the Flagellation, where Christ was bound and scourged before the crucifixion. Distinguish it from the tall architectural column that accompanies Fortitude.

figures.name: The Flagellation
figures.note: among the Arma Christi; the column was venerated as a relic in Rome

symbols.name: cloth bearing an imprinted face
aliases: veil with the face of christ
cloth held open showing a face
symbols.meaning: A cloth held open by its two upper corners, displaying a man's face imprinted on it, is the veil said to have been offered to wipe Christ's face on the road to Calvary and to have retained the image. It stands for an image made without human hands.

figures.name: Saint Veronica
figures.note: shown holding the cloth open toward the viewer

symbols.name: thirty pieces of silver
symbols.meaning: A small bag or scatter of coins numbering thirty is the price of betrayal, paid to Judas and later flung back into the temple. Coins in a betrayal scene read as guilt, not wealth.

figures.name: Judas Iscariot
figures.note: often shown clutching the purse, sometimes with a demon at his ear

symbols.name: Latin cross
aliases: cross with a long lower arm
symbols.meaning: A cross with a longer lower arm, the standard Western form. Held by a saint it signifies faith and the acceptance of suffering; planted in a landscape it marks consecrated ground.

figures.name: Christ
figures.note: the instrument of the crucifixion and the central Christian sign

symbols.name: tau (T-shaped) cross
aliases: cross shaped like the letter T
symbols.meaning: A cross without an upper arm, shaped like the letter T. It is a specific identifying emblem rather than a generic cross, tied to one hermit-saint and the hospital order that took his name.

figures.name: Saint Anthony the Abbot
figures.note: carried as his staff's crosshead; adopted by the Antonine order

symbols.name: X-shaped (saltire) cross
symbols.meaning: A cross of two diagonal beams forming an X. It identifies a specific apostle's martyrdom, who by tradition asked not to die on a cross of the same shape as Christ's, and survives as the flag of Scotland.

figures.name: Saint Andrew
figures.note: his defining attribute; brother of Peter and patron of Scotland

symbols.name: upside-down cross
symbols.meaning: A Latin cross inverted. In Christian iconography this is emphatically not a sign of blasphemy but of humility: it recalls an apostle who asked to be crucified head downward, considering himself unworthy of dying as his master had.

figures.name: Saint Peter
figures.note: his martyrdom under Nero; the inverted cross is a papal emblem

symbols.name: white banner with a red cross
symbols.meaning: A slender staff topped with a white pennant bearing a red cross signals triumph over death. It appears in the hands of the risen Christ, the Lamb of God, and saints associated with resurrection or crusade.

figures.name: The Risen Christ
figures.note: carried at the Resurrection and the Harrowing of Hell

figures.name: The Lamb of God
figures.note: the Agnus Dei is shown supporting this banner

symbols.name: skull
symbols.meaning: A human skull is a memento mori — a blunt reminder of mortality and the brevity of earthly life, prompting reflection and repentance. It appears with penitent figures in the wilderness, with scholars at their desks, and at the center of vanitas still life.

figures.name: Saint Jerome
figures.note: kept in his study as a scholar's reminder of death

figures.name: Saint Mary Magdalene
figures.note: present in scenes of her penitence in the wilderness

figures.name: Golgotha
figures.note: a skull at the foot of the cross marks 'the place of the skull' and Adam's grave

symbols.name: hourglass
symbols.meaning: An hourglass makes time visibly running out, and so is a direct emblem of mortality closely paired with the skull. Its symmetry also lets it stand for the balance of life and death.

figures.name: Vanitas still life
figures.note: a core emblem of the genre

symbols.name: extinguished candle / smoke
symbols.meaning: A candle newly snuffed, its smoke still rising, marks a life or moment just ended — vitality visibly passing away. A lit candle by contrast can signify the presence of Christ or the soul still burning.

figures.name: Vanitas still life
figures.note: a standard emblem of the genre's meditation on mortality

symbols.name: soap bubbles
symbols.meaning: Bubbles, beautiful and certain to burst within seconds, stand for the fragility of life and worldly beauty. The Latin tag 'homo bulla' — man is a bubble — makes the point explicit.

figures.name: Vanitas still life
figures.note: usually paired with a skull or hourglass

symbols.name: book
symbols.meaning: A book signals learning, scripture, or authorship. Open, it suggests active teaching or study and its text may be legible and pointed; closed, contemplation or completed wisdom.

figures.name: The four Evangelists
figures.note: each holds or writes the Gospel attributed to them

figures.name: Saint Jerome
figures.note: signifies his translation of the Bible into Latin

symbols.name: scroll
symbols.meaning: A scroll usually marks an older or prophetic text, distinguishing prophets of the Hebrew Bible from apostles, who typically hold codices. A scroll floating through a scene as a ribbon (banderole) carries the figure's spoken words.

figures.name: Old Testament prophets
figures.note: the scroll marks the older covenant against the apostles' bound books

figures.name: The Archangel Gabriel
figures.note: may carry a banderole reading 'Ave Maria'

symbols.name: quill pen and inkwell
symbols.meaning: A feather pen, often with an inkwell and knife for sharpening, marks a figure as author, scribe, or evangelist caught mid-composition. It turns a portrait into a claim about authorship of the text beside it.

figures.name: The four Evangelists
figures.note: shown writing their Gospels, frequently at divine dictation

figures.name: Saint Jerome
figures.note: at work on the Vulgate translation in his study

symbols.name: keys (two, crossed)
symbols.meaning: A pair of crossed keys, conventionally one gold and one silver, represents the 'keys of the kingdom of heaven' — authority to bind and loose, admit and exclude. They remain the emblem of the papacy.

figures.name: Saint Peter
figures.note: his defining emblem, from Christ's grant of the keys

symbols.name: sword
symbols.meaning: A sword can mark martyrdom by beheading or spiritual warfare — the reading depends on who holds it and what accompanies it. A sword through the neck or held beside a kneeling figure points to execution.

figures.name: Saint Paul
figures.note: both his beheading and the 'sword of the Spirit,' the Word of God

figures.name: Saint Michael
figures.note: a flaming sword for battle against Satan

symbols.name: scales / balance
symbols.meaning: A balance held level represents impartial judgment — weighing right against wrong. In a Last Judgment it is literal: souls are placed in the pans, sometimes with a demon pulling down one side.

figures.name: Saint Michael
figures.note: weighs souls at the Last Judgment

symbols.name: crown
symbols.meaning: A crown marks royal birth or rule, but in martyr imagery it stands instead for the heavenly 'crown of glory' won by death. A crown laid aside or trampled signals renunciation of worldly rank.

figures.name: Saint Catherine of Alexandria
figures.note: reflects her royal birth

figures.name: The Virgin
figures.note: crowned as Queen of Heaven at her Coronation

symbols.name: palm branch
symbols.meaning: A palm frond is the near-universal attribute of Christian martyrdom, signifying victory over death. Because almost any martyr may carry one, it tells you how a saint died but rarely which saint it is.

figures.name: Martyr saints generally
figures.note: the standard generic mark of martyrdom

symbols.name: broken or spiked wheel
symbols.meaning: A wheel studded with spikes, shown broken, recalls a torture device that miraculously shattered before it could kill, forcing execution by another means. It is highly specific rather than generic.

figures.name: Saint Catherine of Alexandria
figures.note: her signature attribute; the source of the 'catherine wheel'

symbols.name: gridiron
symbols.meaning: An iron grate used for roasting marks a martyrdom by fire on a grill. Tradition gives the martyr a famous line to his executioners — that he was done on one side and might be turned — which made him the patron of cooks.

figures.name: Saint Lawrence
figures.note: his defining attribute, usually carried or standing beside him

symbols.name: arrows (piercing a figure)
symbols.meaning: A body pierced by several arrows marks martyrdom by archery, the figure typically bound and serene rather than contorted. Arrows also stand for plague, which is why such images were invoked against epidemics.

figures.name: Saint Sebastian
figures.note: his defining martyrdom — though he survived the arrows and was later clubbed to death

figures.name: Saint Ursula
figures.note: killed by an arrow at Cologne

symbols.name: eyes on a plate or dish
aliases: pair of eyes on a dish
symbols.meaning: A pair of eyes displayed on a dish, separate from the intact face of the figure holding them, is an unmistakable attribute pointing to a martyrdom involving blinding. The saint became patron of eyesight and of the blind.

figures.name: Saint Lucy
figures.note: her name derives from 'lux,' light — the pun is part of the point

symbols.name: severed breasts on a plate
aliases: two round objects on a platter held by a woman
symbols.meaning: Two severed breasts carried on a dish record a specific torture inflicted before death. Because the shapes were later mistaken for loaves or bells, the saint's feast is associated with round breads and with the blessing of bells.

figures.name: Saint Agatha
figures.note: patron against breast disease, fire, and volcanic eruption

symbols.name: pincers holding a tooth
symbols.meaning: A pair of pincers gripping a single tooth records a martyrdom by dental extraction and makes the saint patron of dentists and of those in toothache.

figures.name: Saint Apollonia
figures.note: her teeth were shattered or drawn out during her torture

symbols.name: knife and flayed human skin
aliases: curved knife held by a saint
symbols.meaning: A short curved blade paired with a limp, empty human skin records martyrdom by flaying. Artists sometimes painted their own features into the hanging skin as a signature.

figures.name: Saint Bartholomew
figures.note: flayed alive; patron of tanners and leatherworkers

symbols.name: stones carried or resting on the head
symbols.meaning: Loose stones carried in a book or balanced improbably on the head and shoulders record a death by stoning. The impossible balance is a conventional way of showing the instrument rather than the moment.

figures.name: Saint Stephen
figures.note: the first Christian martyr, shown as a young deacon

symbols.name: severed head on a platter
symbols.meaning: A human head presented on a serving dish depicts an execution granted as a courtly favour rather than a battlefield death — the collision of banquet and beheading is the horror of the image.

figures.name: Saint John the Baptist
figures.note: his head brought to Salome after her dance before Herod

symbols.name: millstone
symbols.meaning: A heavy circular grinding stone, often hung at a figure's neck, records a martyrdom by drowning. It draws on the Gospel warning about a millstone hung about the neck of one who harms the innocent.

figures.name: Saint Vincent of Saragossa
figures.note: cast into the sea with a millstone

figures.name: Saint Christina
figures.note: thrown into a lake bound to a millstone

symbols.name: iron wool comb
symbols.meaning: A spiked iron comb used to card wool, repurposed as an instrument of torture that tore the flesh. It makes its saint the patron of wool-combers as well as of ailments of the throat.

figures.name: Saint Blaise
figures.note: invoked against throat illness; his feast includes the blessing of throats

symbols.name: windlass with entrails
symbols.meaning: A nautical winch around which a martyr's intestines were said to have been wound. The resemblance to a sailor's capstan made the saint a patron of mariners, whose name survives in the electrical glow called St Elmo's fire.

figures.name: Saint Erasmus (Elmo)
figures.note: patron of sailors and of abdominal pain

symbols.name: ointment or alabaster jar
symbols.meaning: A small lidded vessel for perfumed oil recalls an act of anointing — poured over feet in devotion, or brought to a tomb to prepare a body for burial.

figures.name: Saint Mary Magdalene
figures.note: her defining attribute, from her anointing of Christ's feet

figures.name: The Three Marys
figures.note: carry jars to the empty tomb on Easter morning

symbols.name: chalice
symbols.meaning: A stemmed cup stands for the Eucharist and the blood of Christ. Paired with a wafer it signifies the sacrament; held by a personification it marks Faith; catching blood beneath the cross it makes the crucifixion the origin of the Mass.

figures.name: Faith personified
figures.note: holds chalice and cross

figures.name: Saint Barbara
figures.note: a chalice and host allude to dying without last rites

symbols.name: chalice with a serpent
symbols.meaning: A cup with a small snake rising from it records a poisoned drink survived unharmed — the venom made visible as it leaves the vessel, proof of divine protection.

figures.name: Saint John the Evangelist
figures.note: made to drink poison and unaffected by it

symbols.name: monstrance
aliases: sunburst vessel with a white disc
symbols.meaning: A sunburst-shaped vessel on a stem displaying a white wafer behind glass, made to show the consecrated host for adoration. Held up by a saint it usually records the repelling of a threat by the sacrament alone.

figures.name: Saint Clare of Assisi
figures.note: held it up to turn back soldiers threatening her convent

symbols.name: censer / thurible
symbols.meaning: A pierced metal vessel swung on chains to burn incense; the rising smoke stands for prayer ascending. Angels swing censers in heavenly scenes to mark the space as liturgical.

figures.name: Angels
figures.note: censing the Virgin or the altar in devotional images

symbols.name: crozier (crook-topped staff)
symbols.meaning: A tall staff with a spiral crook at the top, shaped after a shepherd's crook, marks a bishop or abbot as pastor of a flock. With a mitre it is the standard pairing for episcopal rank.

figures.name: Bishop saints
figures.note: Nicholas, Ambrose, Augustine, Martin and many others

symbols.name: three gold balls or orbs
aliases: three gold orbs on a book
symbols.meaning: Three small golden spheres recall secret dowries dropped through a window to save three sisters from destitution. The story made the saint a gift-giver and, indirectly, the pawnbroker's sign.

figures.name: Saint Nicholas
figures.note: the origin of both this attribute and the later Santa Claus tradition

symbols.name: pilgrim's staff and scallop shell
aliases: broad hat with a shell badge
symbols.meaning: A long staff, a water gourd, a satchel, and a scallop badge on the hat or cloak identify a pilgrim, historically one returning from the shrine of Santiago de Compostela.

figures.name: Saint James the Greater
figures.note: patron of the Compostela pilgrimage, whose badge the shell became

figures.name: Saint Roch
figures.note: a pilgrim who tended plague victims

symbols.name: scallop shell
symbols.meaning: A large fan-shaped shell is a pilgrim's badge, historically tied to the pilgrimage route to Santiago de Compostela. It is also used as a baptismal vessel, pouring water over the head.

figures.name: Saint James the Greater
figures.note: the badge of the Camino de Santiago

symbols.name: tower
aliases: small tower held in the hand
symbols.meaning: A tower held as an attribute marks a specific imprisonment by a father or captor rather than a generic building. Count the windows if visible — three were said to have been cut into it to honour the Trinity.

figures.name: Saint Barbara
figures.note: patron of miners, gunners, and those at risk of sudden death

symbols.name: anchor
symbols.meaning: An anchor signifies hope — 'an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast' — and steadfastness under storm. Its resemblance to a cross made it an early covert Christian sign, and it also marks martyrdom by drowning.

figures.name: Hope personified
figures.note: her standard attribute, often with eyes raised heavenward

figures.name: Saint Clement
figures.note: said to have been cast into the sea tied to an anchor

symbols.name: ship
symbols.meaning: A ship carrying passengers through rough water is an old image of the Church bearing souls safely across a hostile world — the reason a church's main space is still called the nave, from 'navis.'

figures.name: Saint Ursula
figures.note: sails with her companions to their martyrdom at Cologne

figures.name: The calming of the storm
figures.note: the disciples' boat on the Sea of Galilee

symbols.name: musical instrument (organ, lute, harp)
symbols.meaning: An instrument in a saint's hands marks patronage of sacred music; among angels it signals the harmony of heaven; and in a vanitas still life it stands for pleasure that ends the moment the sound stops.

figures.name: Saint Cecilia
figures.note: patron of music, usually at a small portable organ

figures.name: King David
figures.note: with a harp, as psalmist

symbols.name: trumpet
aliases: long trumpet raised to the lips
symbols.meaning: A trumpet raised by a winged figure proclaims news to the world — triumph, renown, or the summons of the Last Judgment. Fame is sometimes given two, one for praise and one for infamy.

figures.name: Fame personified
figures.note: spreading reputation across the world

figures.name: Angels of the Last Judgment
figures.note: sounding to wake the dead

symbols.name: money purse / coins
symbols.meaning: A bag of money or scattered coins can mean wealth, charity given away, avarice, or payment for treachery — what the figure is doing with it decides which. Coins being handed out read very differently from coins clutched.

figures.name: Saint Lawrence
figures.note: distributed the church's treasure to the poor

figures.name: Saint Matthew
figures.note: recalls his former trade as a tax collector

figures.name: Avarice personified
figures.note: hoards or counts the coins

symbols.name: hourglass with wings
symbols.meaning: An hourglass given wings makes the point that time does not merely pass but flies — 'tempus fugit.' Common on tombs and in vanitas painting.

figures.name: Vanitas and funerary art
figures.note: a compact statement of time's speed and mortality

symbols.name: compass / dividers
symbols.meaning: A pair of dividers stands for measurement, reason, and design — the tool of geometry, architecture, and astronomy. Used of God it presents creation as an act of precise design; lying idle it belongs to melancholy.

figures.name: God the Creator
figures.note: the 'divine architect' measuring out the world

symbols.name: globe or orb
symbols.meaning: A sphere in the hand signifies dominion over the world. Surmounted by a cross it becomes the imperial or royal orb, asserting rule held under God; beneath a figure's feet it can instead mark the world renounced.

figures.name: Christ (Salvator Mundi)
figures.note: holds the globe as saviour and ruler of the world

figures.name: Emperors and kings
figures.note: the orb as a regalia of sovereignty

symbols.name: oil lamp
symbols.meaning: A small oil lamp signifies vigilance and readiness, from the parable of the wise and foolish virgins whose lamps were kept filled or allowed to fail. It also marks the eternal light of a sanctuary.

figures.name: The Wise and Foolish Virgins
figures.note: a lit lamp marks the wise; a spilled or dark one the foolish

symbols.name: rosary
symbols.meaning: A string of beads for counting repeated, meditative prayers. Held by a saint it points to Marian devotion; hanging from a belt it simply marks the figure as religious.

figures.name: Saint Dominic
figures.note: credited by tradition with promoting the rosary

symbols.name: beehive
symbols.meaning: A beehive signifies eloquence — speech as sweet as honey — and also industrious, well-ordered community. A hive at a saint's feet usually points to a legend of bees settling on his mouth in infancy.

figures.name: Saint Ambrose
figures.note: bees were said to have swarmed on his lips, foretelling his eloquence

symbols.name: broken cup
symbols.meaning: A cup shattering, sometimes with a snake leaving it, records poisoned wine destroyed by a blessing before it could be drunk — deliverance made visible in the moment of breaking.

figures.name: Saint Benedict
figures.note: blessed a poisoned cup offered by rebellious monks and it broke apart

symbols.name: small model of a church or city
aliases: miniature church held in the hands
symbols.meaning: A miniature building cradled in the arms identifies a founder, patron, or protector — the donor who paid for the church, or the saint under whose protection a city is placed.

figures.name: Donors and founder-bishops
figures.note: presenting the building they endowed

figures.name: Patron saints of cities
figures.note: holding the town they guard

symbols.name: club
symbols.meaning: A heavy wooden club signifies raw physical strength and victory won by force rather than skill or cunning.

figures.name: Saint Jude
figures.note: a club marks his martyrdom

symbols.name: crescent moon
symbols.meaning: A crescent moon underfoot identifies the apocalyptic 'woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet' from Revelation, read in Christian art as the Virgin — the Immaculate Conception standing triumphant above time and change.

figures.name: The Immaculate Virgin
figures.note: stands on the crescent, crowned with twelve stars

symbols.name: crown of stars
symbols.meaning: A ring of stars — canonically twelve — encircling a woman's head identifies the apocalyptic woman of Revelation, read in Christian art as the Virgin. The number matches the twelve tribes and twelve apostles.

figures.name: The Immaculate Virgin
figures.note: paired with the crescent moon and rays of sun

symbols.name: lion
symbols.meaning: A lion's meaning shifts with what else is nearby: tamed ferocity beside a scholar at his desk, or evangelist symbolism when winged and paired with a book. Check for wings before deciding which.

figures.name: Saint Jerome
figures.note: a tame lion recalls the thorn he drew from its paw

symbols.name: winged lion
symbols.meaning: One of the four evangelist symbols, distinct from an ordinary lion — look for the wings, and often a book beneath the paw. Also the civic emblem of Venice.

figures.name: Saint Mark the Evangelist
figures.note: patron of Venice, whose relics the city claimed

symbols.name: winged ox
symbols.meaning: One of the four evangelist symbols. The ox, a sacrificial animal, identifies the Gospel that most emphasises sacrifice and priesthood.

figures.name: Saint Luke the Evangelist
figures.note: also patron of painters and physicians

symbols.name: eagle
aliases: bird of prey with spread wings
symbols.meaning: An eagle marks the soaring, visionary quality of one Gospel account. It was also believed to gaze directly at the sun, making it a symbol of contemplation and of the Ascension.

figures.name: Saint John the Evangelist
figures.note: for the lofty theology of his Gospel and Revelation

symbols.name: dove
aliases: bird with spread wings above a figure
symbols.meaning: A white dove descending, usually with rays of light, is the Holy Spirit; carrying an olive twig it announces the end of the Flood and peace. Seven doves around a figure represent the gifts of the Spirit.

figures.name: The Holy Spirit
figures.note: descends at the Annunciation, the Baptism, and Pentecost

figures.name: Saint Gregory the Great
figures.note: a dove at his ear dictates his writings

symbols.name: lamb (Agnus Dei)
symbols.meaning: A lamb, particularly one with a halo carrying a small cross or banner, represents Christ as the sacrificial 'Lamb of God' — innocence offered for others. A lamb carried on the shoulders instead makes the carrier the Good Shepherd.

figures.name: Saint John the Baptist
figures.note: points to a lamb, having named Christ the Lamb of God

figures.name: Saint Agnes
figures.note: a lamb accompanies her, punning on her name

symbols.name: fish
symbols.meaning: A fish was an early covert sign for Christ: the Greek word ΙΧΘΥΣ forms an acrostic of 'Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour.' Fish also evoke baptismal water, the miraculous feeding, and the apostles as 'fishers of men'.

figures.name: Christ
figures.note: the ichthys, used as a discreet identifier in periods of persecution

figures.name: Saint Raphael and Tobias
figures.note: carry the fish whose gall restored the father's sight

symbols.name: pelican piercing its breast
aliases: bird feeding young with its own blood
symbols.meaning: A pelican wounding her own breast to feed her young was believed to revive them with her blood, making her an image of Christ's self-sacrifice and of the Eucharist. Frequently carved on altars and lecterns.

figures.name: Christ
figures.note: 'the pelican in her piety,' a standard Eucharistic emblem

symbols.name: phoenix in flames
aliases: bird in a nest of flames
symbols.meaning: A bird consumed by fire and reborn from its own ashes signifies resurrection and immortality. Early Christian writers seized on the legend as a natural argument for the resurrection of the body.

figures.name: Christ
figures.note: an emblem of the Resurrection

symbols.name: unicorn
symbols.meaning: A single-horned beast said to be untameable except by a virgin, in whose lap it would lay its head. It signifies chastity and purity, and in Marian imagery the Incarnation — the untamable made gentle in Mary's lap.

figures.name: The Virgin Mary
figures.note: the 'hunt of the unicorn' allegorises the Incarnation

figures.name: Chastity personified
figures.note: draws her chariot in triumph imagery

symbols.name: stag or deer
aliases: stag with a cross in its antlers
symbols.meaning: A stag drinking or running signifies the soul longing for God — 'as the hart panteth after the water brooks.' A stag with a glowing crucifix between its antlers records a conversion vision experienced while hunting.

figures.name: Saint Eustace and Saint Hubert
figures.note: both converted by a stag bearing a crucifix in its antlers

symbols.name: dog
symbols.meaning: A dog's meaning shifts with what it is doing: fidelity in a portrait — especially at a wife's feet in a marriage picture — a miraculous provider in a saint's legend, or a pun on a founder's name.

figures.name: Saint Roch
figures.note: a dog brought him bread while he suffered plague in isolation

figures.name: Saint Dominic
figures.note: a dog with a torch puns on 'Domini canis,' hound of the Lord

figures.name: Marriage portraits
figures.note: signifies marital fidelity

symbols.name: rooster / cock
symbols.meaning: A crowing cock marks the moment a predicted failure comes true and is instantly recognised — remorse arriving with daybreak. It is also an emblem of vigilance and of the dawn, and belongs among the instruments of the Passion.

figures.name: Saint Peter
figures.note: recalls his three denials of Christ before the cock crowed

symbols.name: raven or crow
symbols.meaning: A black bird bringing food records miraculous provision in the wilderness, echoing the ravens that fed Elijah; carrying something away it can instead mean the removal of danger. Otherwise ravens read as ill omen and death.

figures.name: Saint Benedict
figures.note: a raven carried off a poisoned loaf at his command

figures.name: Saint Paul the Hermit
figures.note: fed daily by a raven bringing bread

symbols.name: goldfinch
aliases: small bird with a red face
little bird held by a child
symbols.meaning: A small bird with a red patch on its face, held or tethered by the Christ Child. Because it feeds among thorns and thistles it was linked to the crown of thorns, so the child's plaything foreshadows the Passion.

figures.name: The Christ Child
figures.note: an extremely common motif in Italian Madonna and Child paintings

symbols.name: serpent / snake
symbols.meaning: A snake's meaning depends on what it is doing: temptation and the Fall when coiled in a tree, healing when wound on a staff, and evil defeated when crushed underfoot.

figures.name: The Temptation of Eve
figures.note: coiled around the tree, sometimes given a human head

symbols.name: dragon
symbols.meaning: A dragon represents Satan, sin, or chaos to be conquered — speared, trampled, or led on a leash as an allegory of good defeating evil. A dragon subdued rather than killed indicates a saint who tamed rather than fought it.

figures.name: Saint George
figures.note: slain to rescue a princess; faith conquering sin

figures.name: Saint Michael
figures.note: cast down underfoot in the war in heaven

figures.name: Saint Margaret of Antioch
figures.note: emerges unharmed from the dragon that swallowed her

symbols.name: pig
symbols.meaning: A pig at a hermit's feet, often with a bell at its neck, refers to the hospital order permitted to let its pigs forage freely in medieval towns. In other settings a pig signifies gluttony or lust.

figures.name: Saint Anthony the Abbot
figures.note: his pig and bell come from the Antonine order's privileges

symbols.name: hare or rabbit
symbols.meaning: Rabbits, proverbially fertile, usually signify lust and fecundity. A white rabbit at the Virgin's feet reverses this into purity — desire mastered rather than indulged.

figures.name: The Virgin Mary
figures.note: a white rabbit signifies chastity overcoming the flesh

symbols.name: cat
symbols.meaning: In European painting cats generally carry a negative charge — deceit, stealth, lust, or heresy. A cat lurking at the Last Supper or in an Annunciation is usually a deliberate note of menace rather than domestic detail.

figures.name: Judas
figures.note: a cat is sometimes placed near him at the Last Supper

symbols.name: fly
symbols.meaning: A fly rendered with startling realism signifies decay, mortality, and sometimes evil — the insect of corruption placed on fresh flowers or fruit. It doubles as a display of the painter's skill, appearing to sit on the picture's surface.

figures.name: Vanitas and still life
figures.note: a reminder that what is depicted is already rotting

symbols.name: ox and ass at a manger
aliases: cow and donkey beside a crib
symbols.meaning: An ox and a donkey flanking a newborn in a feeding trough are not in the Gospel accounts at all; they enter Nativity imagery from the prophet Isaiah — 'the ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib' — as witnesses recognising what people did not.

figures.name: The Nativity
figures.note: a near-universal fixture of the scene despite its non-scriptural origin

symbols.name: wolf
symbols.meaning: A wolf usually signifies rapacity and threat — the predator of the flock, and so of heresy or the devil. A wolf shown docile beside a saint reverses this, marking violence reconciled rather than destroyed.

figures.name: Saint Francis of Assisi
figures.note: made peace with the wolf that terrorised Gubbio

symbols.name: fox
symbols.meaning: A fox signifies cunning, fraud, and — in religious contexts — heresy, from the 'little foxes that spoil the vines' of the Song of Songs, read as heretics damaging the Church.

figures.name: Allegories of deceit
figures.note: also the trickster fox of medieval beast fable

symbols.name: lily
symbols.meaning: A white lily signifies purity and virginity. In an Annunciation it is the specific sign that conception occurs without loss of virginity; carried by other saints it marks chastity of life.

figures.name: The Virgin Mary
figures.note: her flower, and the reason for the name 'madonna lily'

figures.name: The Archangel Gabriel
figures.note: carries it when announcing the Incarnation

figures.name: Saint Anthony of Padua
figures.note: holds a lily with the Christ Child

symbols.name: rose
symbols.meaning: A red rose signifies love and, in martyrdom, blood shed; a white rose purity. Mary is called the 'rose without thorns' because she was held to be free of original sin, so a thornless rose is a deliberate theological detail.

figures.name: The Virgin Mary
figures.note: the rose garden and rosary both take their name from her flower

symbols.name: iris
symbols.meaning: An iris, whose blade-shaped leaves gave it the name 'sword lily,' stands for the Virgin's sorrows — the sword foretold as piercing her soul. In Netherlandish painting it often substitutes for the lily.

figures.name: The Virgin Mary
figures.note: combines her purity with the prophecy of grief

symbols.name: columbine
symbols.meaning: A columbine takes its name from the Latin for dove, which its inverted petals resemble. It therefore signifies the Holy Spirit, and a plant of seven blooms represents the Spirit's seven gifts.

figures.name: The Holy Spirit
figures.note: frequently placed in Annunciation and Nativity foregrounds

symbols.name: pomegranate
symbols.meaning: A pomegranate split to show its packed seeds signifies the unity of the many within one Church, and — because it was Persephone's fruit and returns each spring — resurrection and eternal life. Held by the Christ Child it points to the Passion and what follows it.

figures.name: The Christ Child
figures.note: a common alternative to the goldfinch in Madonna paintings

symbols.name: apple
aliases: round fruit held in the hand
symbols.meaning: An apple signifies the Fall and original sin — the Latin pun between 'malum' (evil) and 'malum' (apple) helped fix the association. In the Christ Child's or the Virgin's hand it reverses into redemption: the fruit that caused the Fall, held by the one who undoes it.

figures.name: Adam and Eve
figures.note: the fruit of the tree of knowledge, though Genesis never names it

symbols.name: grapes / vine
symbols.meaning: Grapes and vine leaves carry the Eucharist and Christ's words 'I am the true vine.' Grapes paired with wheat are unmistakably Eucharistic — wine and bread together.

figures.name: Christ
figures.note: the true vine; the blood of the Eucharist

symbols.name: ears of wheat
symbols.meaning: Stalks of wheat signify bread and so, with grapes, the Eucharist — Christ's body given as food.

figures.name: Christ / the Eucharist
figures.note: the bread of the sacrament, paired with the vine

symbols.name: olive branch
symbols.meaning: An olive branch signifies peace and reconciliation, from the twig the dove carried back to Noah's ark, showing God's wrath had passed.

figures.name: The dove of Noah
figures.note: announcing the receding flood and God's peace

symbols.name: thistle
symbols.meaning: A thistle signifies earthly sorrow and the curse of labour — 'thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee' — and by extension Christ's Passion, since thorns crowned him.

figures.name: The Passion
figures.note: often paired with the goldfinch, which feeds on thistles

symbols.name: carnation / pink
symbols.meaning: A carnation signifies betrothal and love, and in devotional pictures the Passion — its old name 'nail flower' likened the buds to the nails of the crucifixion. A carnation in a portrait usually marks an engagement.

figures.name: Betrothal portraits
figures.note: held between finger and thumb to signal a marriage contract

symbols.name: violet
symbols.meaning: A violet, low-growing and half-hidden, signifies humility and modesty — the virtue that does not display itself. It is a frequent attribute of the Virgin's humility.

figures.name: The Virgin Mary
figures.note: 'the violet of humility' in devotional literature

symbols.name: strawberry
aliases: small red berries with white flowers
symbols.meaning: A strawberry, which flowers white and fruits red on the same plant and has no stone or thorn, signifies righteousness and the fruits of the Spirit. Its three-part leaf was also read as the Trinity.

figures.name: Paradise imagery
figures.note: carpets the foreground of 'garden of paradise' paintings

symbols.name: cypress tree
symbols.meaning: A cypress signifies death and mourning — it was planted in classical burial grounds and, once cut, does not regrow. Because it is evergreen it simultaneously suggests life beyond death.

figures.name: Funerary imagery
figures.note: still the characteristic tree of Mediterranean cemeteries

symbols.name: palm tree
symbols.meaning: A whole palm tree signifies victory, righteousness, and paradise — 'the righteous shall flourish like the palm tree.' Distinguish it from a cut palm frond carried in the hand, which specifically marks martyrdom.

figures.name: The Rest on the Flight into Egypt
figures.note: a palm bends to offer its dates to the Holy Family

symbols.name: walled or enclosed garden
symbols.meaning: A garden shut in by a wall or fence, often with a sealed fountain, is the 'hortus conclusus' of the Song of Songs — 'a garden enclosed is my sister, my spouse.' It is a figure for the Virgin's intact virginity.

figures.name: The Virgin Mary
figures.note: usually shown seated within it, sometimes with a unicorn

symbols.name: red robe
symbols.meaning: Red signifies the blood of martyrdom, divine love, and burning zeal. It is also the colour of cardinals and, in Christ's case, of the mock royal robe of the Passion and the garment of the Resurrection.

figures.name: Christ
figures.note: wears red beneath a blue mantle, or the mock purple-red of the mockery

figures.name: Martyrs
figures.note: red vestments mark martyrs' feasts in the liturgical calendar

symbols.name: blue mantle
symbols.meaning: Blue signifies heaven, truth, and constancy. Because true ultramarine was ground from lapis lazuli imported at enormous cost, giving a figure a blue mantle was also a visible statement of expense and honour.

figures.name: The Virgin Mary
figures.note: her near-universal colour; contracts often specified the grade of blue to be used

symbols.name: white garment
symbols.meaning: White signifies purity, innocence, and glory. Dazzling white marks transfigured or resurrected bodies and the robes of the redeemed; it is also the habit colour of several religious orders.

figures.name: The Risen Christ and angels
figures.note: 'his raiment was white as the light' at the Transfiguration

symbols.name: purple garment
symbols.meaning: Purple signifies imperial rank and, in the liturgy, penitence and mourning. Because true Tyrian purple was ruinously expensive it was restricted to emperors, which is what makes the purple robe of the mockery a cruel joke.

figures.name: Christ mocked
figures.note: dressed in purple as a false king before the crucifixion

symbols.name: black garment
symbols.meaning: Black signifies death, mourning, and renunciation of the world; it is the habit colour of several orders and, in Spanish and Dutch portraiture, a mark of sober piety and considerable wealth — good black dye was expensive.

figures.name: Benedictines and Dominicans
figures.note: the 'black monks'; Dominicans wear a black cloak over white

symbols.name: gold background
symbols.meaning: A flat, spaceless field of gold leaf behind a figure removes the scene from ordinary place and time, standing for divine, eternal light rather than any sky. Its abandonment for landscape backgrounds marks one of the great shifts into Renaissance painting.

figures.name: Byzantine and medieval panel painting
figures.note: the standard setting for sacred figures before naturalistic space

symbols.name: yellow garment
symbols.meaning: Yellow is unstable in meaning: gold-yellow can signify divine light and revelation, but a dull or acid yellow frequently marks treachery, envy, and deceit — most notoriously as the colour given to Judas in Italian painting.

figures.name: Judas Iscariot
figures.note: conventionally robed in yellow to mark him as the betrayer

symbols.name: cardinal's hat
symbols.meaning: A broad-brimmed red hat with hanging tassels marks the rank of cardinal. It is often included anachronistically, applied to figures who lived long before the office existed as a mark of later honour.

figures.name: Saint Jerome
figures.note: given the hat retrospectively; he was never a cardinal in the modern sense

symbols.name: bishop's mitre
symbols.meaning: A tall, cleft, peaked cap worn by bishops and abbots. Paired with a crozier it is the standard signal of episcopal rank, and can be shown laid aside to indicate humility or an office refused.

figures.name: Bishop saints
figures.note: Nicholas, Augustine, Martin, Ambrose and others

symbols.name: papal tiara
symbols.meaning: A tall conical crown ringed by three coronets identifies the pope. The three tiers were read as three orders of authority, and the tiara appears with crossed keys as the papal arms.

figures.name: Saint Peter and papal saints
figures.note: anachronistic for Peter but used to assert his primacy

symbols.name: deacon's dalmatic
symbols.meaning: A wide-sleeved tunic with vertical bands, worn over the alb, marks a deacon rather than a priest or bishop. Young saints in dalmatics are almost always the martyr-deacons.

figures.name: Saint Stephen and Saint Lawrence
figures.note: both deacons, usually shown young and beardless in dalmatics

symbols.name: brown habit with a knotted cord
aliases: brown monk's robe with rope belt
symbols.meaning: A coarse brown or grey habit tied with a knotted rope identifies a Franciscan. The three knots stand for the vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience, and the cheap undyed cloth is itself the point.

figures.name: Saint Francis and Saint Anthony of Padua
figures.note: the order's founder and its most popular preacher

symbols.name: white habit with a black cloak
aliases: white robe under a black cape
symbols.meaning: A white tunic and scapular under a black hooded cloak identifies a Dominican — the 'black friars' of preaching and, later, of the Inquisition.

figures.name: Saint Dominic and Saint Thomas Aquinas
figures.note: the order's founder and its greatest theologian

symbols.name: camel hair garment
symbols.meaning: A rough garment of animal hair signals ascetic hardship and life in the wilderness — deliberate austerity rather than poverty imposed.

figures.name: Saint John the Baptist
figures.note: his described dress while preaching in the desert

symbols.name: ermine-trimmed robe
symbols.meaning: White fur dotted with black tail-tips marks the highest rank — reserved by sumptuary law in many places to royalty, high nobility, and judges. It signals status and, through the animal's reputation, incorruptibility.

figures.name: Royal and noble portraits
figures.note: still used in coronation and judicial dress

symbols.name: turban
symbols.meaning: A wound cloth headdress is used by European painters to mark a figure as Eastern, ancient, or foreign — applied to Old Testament patriarchs, magi, and Roman officials alike as a generic sign of 'elsewhere and long ago' rather than accurate costume.

figures.name: The Magi
figures.note: marks them as wise men from the East

figures.name: Old Testament figures
figures.note: a conventional signal of antiquity and the Orient

symbols.name: armor
symbols.meaning: Armor marks a soldier, a soldier-saint, or spiritual warfare — 'the whole armour of God.' On an allegorical figure it usually signifies fortitude or just war rather than actual soldiering.

figures.name: Saint George and Saint Michael
figures.note: the two great armored dragon-slayers

symbols.name: Annunciation
aliases: angel appearing to a kneeling woman
angel with a lily approaching a woman at a book
symbols.meaning: A winged messenger approaches a woman interrupted at her reading, usually with a lily, a descending dove, and rays of light. It depicts the announcement that she will bear Christ, and the whole scene turns on her assent.

figures.name: The Archangel Gabriel and the Virgin Mary
figures.note: the most frequently painted moment in Christian art

symbols.name: Nativity
aliases: infant in a stable with animals
symbols.meaning: A newborn laid in a feeding trough in a stable or cave, attended by his mother, an ox and an ass, and often shepherds. Light frequently radiates from the child himself, making him the source of illumination in the scene.

figures.name: The Holy Family
figures.note: Joseph is often placed to one side, aged and asleep or in shadow

symbols.name: Adoration of the Magi
aliases: wise men kneeling before a child
magi with gold frankincense and myrrh
symbols.meaning: Three richly dressed travellers present gold, frankincense, and myrrh to a child on his mother's lap, the eldest usually kneeling and bare-headed. The gifts were read as kingship, divinity, and death — the myrrh a burial spice foreshadowing the Passion.

figures.name: The Magi
figures.note: shown as three ages of man and, from the late Middle Ages, three continents

symbols.name: Baptism of Christ
aliases: figure standing in a river being baptized
water poured over a man's head in a river
symbols.meaning: A man stands in a river while another pours water over his head, a dove descends, and the heavens open. It marks the start of Christ's public ministry and is one of the clearest depictions of the Trinity together.

figures.name: Christ and Saint John the Baptist
figures.note: John in camel hair, often with a shallow bowl or shell

symbols.name: Last Supper
aliases: thirteen men at a long table
symbols.meaning: Thirteen men at a table sharing bread and wine — simultaneously the institution of the Eucharist and the announcement that one present will betray. Painters usually choose which of the two moments to depict, and the betrayer is often isolated by pose, shadow, or a money bag.

figures.name: Christ and the twelve apostles
figures.note: Judas marked by the purse, a shadow, or yellow robes

symbols.name: Agony in the Garden
aliases: man praying at night while others sleep
kneeling figure with an angel holding a cup
symbols.meaning: A figure kneels in prayer at night while his companions sleep nearby, sometimes with an angel presenting a chalice. It depicts the moment of dread before arrest — the cup being the suffering asked to pass.

figures.name: Christ at Gethsemane
figures.note: the sleeping apostles are Peter, James, and John

symbols.name: Crucifixion
aliases: figure on a cross with mourners
symbols.meaning: A figure fixed to a cross, usually with the INRI board above, mourners at the foot, and a darkened sky. A skull at the base marks the site as 'the place of the skull'; a chalice catching blood makes the scene the origin of the Mass.

figures.name: Christ
figures.note: flanked by the Virgin and Saint John, with the Magdalene often at the foot

symbols.name: Deposition / Descent from the Cross
aliases: body being lowered from a cross
men on ladders taking down a body
symbols.meaning: The dead body lowered from the cross with ladders and a winding sheet, supported by helpers below. The composition typically stresses dead weight and the awkward physical labour of grief.

figures.name: Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus
figures.note: the two men who requested and prepared the body

symbols.name: Pietà
aliases: dead man across a seated woman's lap
symbols.meaning: A seated woman holding the dead body of a grown man across her lap. Unlike the Deposition it depicts no narrative moment in the Gospels but a devotional image invented to invite contemplation of shared suffering — deliberately echoing a mother holding an infant.

figures.name: The Virgin and the dead Christ
figures.note: a German devotional invention that spread across Europe

symbols.name: Resurrection
aliases: man stepping out of a sarcophagus
symbols.meaning: A figure rises or steps from an opened tomb, usually carrying a white banner with a red cross, while guards sleep or recoil below. The wounds remain visible — the risen body is the same body.

figures.name: The Risen Christ
figures.note: often shown mid-air above the sarcophagus

symbols.name: Last Judgment
aliases: souls divided to left and right
christ judging with the blessed and damned
symbols.meaning: A great composition with a judge enthroned at centre, the blessed rising on his right and the damned dragged down on his left, angels sounding trumpets and often weighing souls. Its rigid left-right division makes the whole picture an argument.

figures.name: Christ the Judge
figures.note: typically showing his wounds; the Virgin and Baptist intercede beside him

symbols.name: Coronation of the Virgin
aliases: figure placing a crown on a kneeling woman
symbols.meaning: A woman kneels or is enthroned in heaven while Christ, or the Trinity, sets a crown on her head. It closes the Marian cycle by making her Queen of Heaven after the Assumption.

figures.name: The Virgin Mary
figures.note: surrounded by musical angels and ranks of saints

symbols.name: Sacra Conversazione
aliases: virgin and child surrounded by saints in one space
symbols.meaning: The Virgin and Child enthroned with saints gathered informally around them in a single unified space — figures from different centuries sharing one room without narrative. It replaced the older format of saints boxed into separate panels.

figures.name: The Virgin, Child, and attendant saints
figures.note: the saints are identified by their individual attributes

symbols.name: Madonna and Child
symbols.meaning: A seated woman holding an infant, the central devotional image of Western art. Variants carry distinct meanings: the child reaching for the breast, the two cheeks pressed together in tenderness, or the mother gesturing formally toward him as 'the way'.

figures.name: The Virgin and Christ Child
figures.note: objects in the child's hand — goldfinch, pomegranate, fruit — usually foreshadow the Passion

symbols.name: vanitas still life
aliases: arrangement of skull books and candle
table of objects with a skull
symbols.meaning: An arrangement of objects assembled to argue that everything shown is passing: a skull and hourglass for death, snuffed candles and bubbles for brevity, books and instruments for learning and pleasure that end, coins and jewels for wealth left behind.

figures.name: Dutch and Flemish still life
figures.note: the genre's name comes from 'vanity of vanities, all is vanity'

symbols.name: angel
symbols.meaning: A winged human figure serving as messenger, guardian, or attendant of the divine. Angels mark a scene as taking place across the boundary between heaven and earth, and their number, dress, and activity — announcing, censing, playing music, or bearing instruments of the Passion — tell you what kind of moment it is.

figures.name: The Archangel Gabriel
figures.note: the messenger of the Annunciation, usually with a lily

figures.name: The Archangel Michael
figures.note: armed and armored, weighing souls or defeating the dragon

symbols.name: putto / cherub
symbols.meaning: A plump winged infant, borrowed from classical art. In sacred pictures putti attend the divine and soften it; in secular ones they accompany love and abundance. A winged child's head with no body represents a cherub as pure intellect without physical needs.

figures.name: Sacred and secular decoration
figures.note: distinct from Cupid, who carries a bow and arrows

symbols.name: six-winged angel (seraph)
symbols.meaning: An angel with three pairs of wings, often red and covering its own face and feet, belongs to the highest rank of the heavenly hierarchy. Its appearance signals a vision of the divine presence rather than an ordinary errand.

figures.name: Saint Francis of Assisi
figures.note: received the stigmata from a crucified seraph
